title: Anand Sahib: the song of bliss
hook: forty pauris of joy found through the Guru, closing every Sikh gathering

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chaupai Sahib closed, and your line was keep me. Now a new bani begins, the one Sikhs sing together.

At a Sikh wedding, the couple walks slowly around the Guru Granth Sahib four times while the four verses called the Laavan are sung. Then the music shifts. Before the final prayer, the whole room joins in a song: grandparents, cousins, friends who flew in, kids who've been fidgeting for an hour. The same song closes the ordinary Sunday service, a baby's naming, and a funeral. And the wedding shares its first word: the ceremony is called Anand Karaj, the ceremony of bliss.
screen: `FOUR ROUNDS, THE LAAVAN SUNG.` → `THEN THE WHOLE ROOM SINGS.` → `ANAND KARAJ: THE CEREMONY OF BLISS.`

segments.voice: Anand means bliss, a deep, settled joy. Anand Sahib is a bani by Guru Amar Das, the third Guru, in Raag Ramkali, set in the Guru Granth Sahib: forty pauris, forty stanzas. You first met it on day one hundred thirty-three; now comes the slow walk through it, the way the Japji and Chaupai went. Two forms matter. Many Sikhs say all forty pauris in the morning, as one of the five banis of the Nitnem. And a short form, the first five pauris and the last, six in all, closes nearly every Sikh gathering, followed by the Ardas. Sikh tradition tells that Guru Amar Das composed it when a grandson was born to his family, and the child was named Anand. Whether or not every detail is exact, the story fits: this song comes out of a family's joy. And it's rarely a solo. It's the song a room sings. A wedding sings it on the way into a marriage; a funeral sings it on the way through grief. The same words, in both rooms. That says something about anand in this tradition. It isn't the high of a good day. It's a joy deep enough to be sung beside a coffin as well as beside a bride, a joy that can hold sorrow without breaking. And it's found, the song will say, through the Guru.
screen: `ANAND: DEEP, SETTLED JOY.` · `FORTY PAURIS; SIX CLOSE EVERY GATHERING.` · `BORN, TRADITION SAYS, OF A FAMILY'S JOY.` · `SUNG AT WEDDINGS AND FUNERALS ALIKE.` · then, large: `BLISS, TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: If you can, play a recording of the short Anand Sahib, the six pauris sung at the close of a Sikh service; it takes only a few minutes. Don't work at the words yet; just breathe with the sound of many voices singing one thing. If you can't play it now, picture a room full of people you love singing together, and if you pray, join with Waheguru at the end.
Anand. Bliss, a deep and settled joy; Guru Amar Das's forty-pauri song, whose six pauris close nearly every Sikh gathering, weddings and funerals alike.
Your line: bliss, together. Six pauris, many voices, and one song between them. Day three hundred eighty.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite all forty pauris of Anand Sahib in the morning Nitnem, and the first five pauris with the fortieth are sung at the close of nearly every Sikh service and ceremony, before the Ardas.

chat.says: I went to a Sikh wedding and a Sikh funeral. Why did they sing the same song?
options: Anand Sahib sings a deep joy, found through the Guru, that can hold sorrow too.
It's the only hymn Sikhs have, so it simply gets used at every event.
The funeral version is a sad rewrite; only the old tune stays the same.
chat.meaning: Anand means a deep, settled joy. The same six pauris close weddings and funerals, because this joy can hold sorrow without breaking.
